title: Krishna Reports the Failure of Peace
story:
Krishna's chariot rolled into Upaplavya, and the report of the peace mission came with it. He had gone to Hastinapura to ask for peace in the name of the Pandavas, and now he told them everything that had happened there, and sat long in consultation with them. Then, wearied, he went to his own quarters for rest.

The Pandavas dismissed the kings who had gathered around them, with Virata at their head. When the sun had set, they said their evening prayers, their hearts fixed on Krishna, thinking of him. At last they brought him into their midst again and deliberated once more on what they should do. It was Yudhishthira who spoke first, addressing him as one addresses a refuge: "O you of lotus-petal eyes, tell us all that you said to Dhritarashtra's son in the assembly of the Kurus."

Krishna's answer was brief and final. "Having gone to the city of Hastinapura," he said, "I addressed Dhritarashtra's son in the assembly with words that were true, reasonable, and beneficial. That wicked-minded fellow did not accept them."

The mission had failed. But Yudhishthira did not want the summary; he wanted everything. When Duryodhana chose the wrong path, what had the aged grandsire said? What had the preceptor Drona, the son of Bharadwaja, said? What had Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, his own parents, said? What had Kshattri, Vidura, their junior father, foremost of all who knew virtue, always afflicted with sorrow for them, whom he regarded as his own sons, said? And what had all the kings who sat in that assembly said? "Tell us all of it exactly as it happened," Yudhishthira said. "You have already told us the disagreeable words of the Kuru chiefs, but they have flitted from my memory. I want to hear them again. You are our refuge, our lord, our guide."

So Krishna began, and the night closed over Upaplavya while he spoke. "Hear, O king, the words that were addressed to Duryodhana in the midst of the assembly of the Kurus, and bear them in mind. After my words were ended, Dhritarashtra's son laughed aloud."

That laugh had decided more than the assembly knew. Highly incensed, Bhishma had risen and spoken for the preservation of their race. He reminded Duryodhana of the vow he himself had taken, how for his father Santanu's sake he had procured Kali to become his mother and had renounced the throne, so that an only son might not be the end of the line; how Vichitravirya had been born and installed as king while Bhishma served under him; how, when Vichitravirya died and anarchy seized the realm, the chief of the gods withheld rain until the starving subjects, afflicted with frightful maladies, begged Bhishma to take the throne for their sake, and he had refused, keeping his vow. And now, Bhishma said, the line he had sacrificed his own kingship to preserve was being led toward ruin by the very prince who carried it.

And the recounting had only begun. The night stretched on, and Krishna's voice carried that assembly into the quiet camp, the laughter, the anger, the pleadings of parents and preceptor and grandsire, all the words that peace had been unable to make true. The Pandavas knew now, in full, what they had known in outline: nothing remained to be said about peace, and they would carry this story with them onto the field of Kurukshetra.
reflection: Yudhishthira's insistence on hearing the assembly's words exactly, even a second time, shows how much the telling matters on the eve of war: the brothers cannot move forward until they know precisely what was said and who said it. The failure of the mission becomes, in Krishna's retelling, a story the Pandavas will carry with them to the battlefield.
next_story_tease: Peace had failed, and the battles to come would bring Krishna to Arjuna's side once more.
hero_scene: In the lamplit night at Upaplavya, Krishna sits in the midst of the five Pandava brothers and begins his report of the failed mission, while Yudhishthira leans forward, listening with fixed attention.

Yudhishthira asking Krishna to tell everything that was said
Krishna seated among the five brothers, beginning his account
